title: The AI Code Paradox: Why Software is Becoming 'Write-Only' and Disposable
summary: Artificial intelligence is ushering in an era where software code becomes inherently 'write-only' due to its extreme density, making it virtually unreadable by humans. This shift means debugging is increasingly replaced by rewriting, and testing evolves into the primary form of documentation, fundamentally altering traditional software engineering practices.
content:
Imagine a future where the very building blocks of our digital world — code — become indecipherable to human eyes, relegated to a 'write-only' status. This isn't a dystopian fantasy, but a stark reality predicted by Phillip Mortimer at QCon London, where he argued that artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming software engineering into an era of opaque, disposable code.

Mortimer's central contention is that AI-generated code is simply too dense, too complex, for human developers to effectively read or review at scale. In this paradigm, traditional code comprehension becomes a futile exercise. Instead, the behavior of software is defined and understood almost exclusively through its tests, which effectively evolve into the primary — and perhaps only — reliable form of documentation. This radical shift demands a re-evaluation of how we approach software quality assurance and understanding.

Furthermore, the AI era also ushers in what Mortimer terms 'disposable' code. The sheer difficulty and time investment required to debug intricate, AI-generated solutions will often outweigh the effort of simply prompting the AI to rewrite the entire segment. This means the classic developer dilemma of 'debug or refactor' morphs into 'debug or regenerate,' leaning heavily towards the latter, fundamentally altering the economics and timelines of software maintenance. Human intervention, in this context, moves away from meticulous line-by-line review to higher-level architectural guidance and test formulation.

This profound transformation poses critical questions for the future of software development. How do we ensure ethical considerations are baked into systems when their underlying codebases are largely impenetrable? What becomes of mentorship, code quality standards, and the human expertise cultivated over decades? While AI promises unprecedented speed and capability, Mortimer's insights force us to confront the trade-offs: a future of rapid iteration, perhaps, but one built on foundations increasingly alien to the human mind.
keyTakeaways: AI-generated code is often too dense and complex for humans to effectively read or review, rendering it 'write-only'.
Tests are becoming the primary form of documentation and definition of behavior for AI-generated code, replacing traditional human-readable documentation.
Code is increasingly 'disposable'; it's often more efficient to rewrite or regenerate AI-generated code than to debug complex issues within it.
author: Ben Linders
